#8329. Hunting Like a Cheesehead Is the Best Way to Spend Your Deer Season

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 10:32 AM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Author’s Note: This story was originally published in 2020, and Gramps is gone now. After his funeral, we buried his ashes in the woods beneath his stand. A small cross my dad built sits atop the hill where he shot the buck in this story. I think of our hunt that morning, and all of the good times spent hunting and fishing with my grandpa, every time that I pass it.

The boom comes from the southeast, and it’s loud enough to startle me in my treestand. On opening day of deer season in northern Wisconsin, the woods come alive with gunfire: soft pops in the distance, sharp cracks from the neighbors’ properties, and hurried four- or five-shot strings from someone hammering away with a lever gun at deer bounding across a cornfield. But a bang loud enough to reverberate off the tree I’m sitting in? That has to be Grampa’s .300 Win. Mag.

This is my twentieth season hunting our family land—a few hundred acres of mixed timber where we pack in four or five Robinsons each fall weekend to hunt deer. Because there’s limited room to roam, we all have designated stands that change only occasionally from year to year. Gramps has been hunting the same 3 acres for more than a decade.

This deer hunting strategy—sitting in your stand day after day until you kill a deer or the season ends—is the polar ­opposite of the highly mobile trend of tree saddles and cellular trail cameras. Today’s run-and-gun deer hunter must be agile and adaptive, constantly reading conditions and efficiently changing setups. And sure, that style of hunting can be fun and effective. But at our camp, change comes more slowly.

A few years ago, for example, I tried to get everyone to use trail cameras. While they all agreed it was cool to see pictures of deer and other wildlife, the consensus was that the cameras kind of ruined the magic of it all. My dad said that if he knew a big buck was out there, then killed a smaller buck, he might feel disappointed. And when I brought a new pour-over coffeemaker to camp, I upset the long tradition of our blue enamel percolators, which either take too long to perk or heat too quickly and boil over. Even though they’re the source of constant bickering each morning, I was ridiculed as some kind of newfangled French barista. ­(Explaining that the pour-over method was invented by a German woman in the 1900s didn’t help my case.)

Two years ago, Gramps shot a small buck with his .300 but didn’t have the gun mounted solidly to his shoulder. The scope slammed into his face and busted his nose so badly he had to check into the ER to stop the bleeding; that summer, my dad and my uncle Pat tried to talk Gramps into shooting a .243 for deer hunting. But on opening weekend Gramps had his big .300 back at camp.

“Ack, don’t be wimps,” he said, ignoring everyone’s looks of concern. “It’s just a little kick.”

Ack, don’t be wimps. It’s just a little kick.

You could view this never-change ­attitude as a special kind of stubbornness. Or, more generously, the best kind of perseverance. This is the same attitude that has allowed three generations of Robinsons to master the art of sitting in the woods. That might sound unimpressive because, of course, almost all hunters sit in the woods. But when I got older and started deer hunting with folks outside my family, I noticed subtle differences in how other people hunted. Other deer hunters bring books to read in their blinds or look at their phones to fight boredom. They shuffle around in their seats, sneak naps, and check their watches. Anything to pass the time, like they’re trying to fast-forward the hunt to the good parts. I suspect these are the same people who complain that they’re too busy and that the days fly by too quickly.

But when the Robinsons are deer hunting, we don’t want time to pass. We’re happy to watch a squirrel or a grouse, or just listen to the geese migrate until it’s time for lunch, a buck appears, or the sun sets on the day.

I’ve had the opportunity to interview some of the best deer hunters in the country, and they’ve shared mountains of tactics and knowledge with me. But I learned the big lesson, the one that matters most, at our family deer camp as a kid. There’s real value in sitting still, being quiet, and happily waiting for a thing that may never come.

Read Next: The Case for New, Wood-Stocked Deer Hunting Rifles

At lunchtime I climb down, fire up my four-wheeler, and drive to Grampa’s stand. My cousin Shawn pulls up at the same time, and we walk toward the voices we hear echoing through the popple. We find my dad, who beat us there, and Gramps standing over a beautiful 10-point with a golf ball-size hole blown through its chest. Gramps tells the story with a look on his face that I can only describe as, “See, told ya.”

Dad casually mentions that he also killed a buck that morning, so once we get Gramps’ deer to camp, he and I set out to retrieve it. From maybe 80 yards away I can see a massive rack sticking up from the fallen leaves.

“Holy smokes,” I mutter as my dad hoists the antlers of an enormous northwoods 8-pointer. It’s the best buck he’s ever killed, and also the largest buck we’ve ever taken—or even seen—on our land. “He’s a pretty nice one,” he tells me as we lash the buck to his wheeler. “But I didn’t want to take away from Grampa’s big moment.”

By next fall, 80-year-old Gramps will be one year older, and my dad will have major back surgery that limits his hunting for the season. Change will come for the Robinson deer camp whether we like it or not.

Related: This Is How the Boomer Generation Shaped Hunting Culture, for Better and Worse

But now isn’t the time to worry about any of that. We have to hang the bucks on the meat pole and get the brats ready for lunch. That, after all, is our tradition.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

In Spain’s emptying countryside, nature is moving back in.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

#8321. Senate Passes BAAJA, the Massive Permitting Bill That Will Expedite Development on Public Lands

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 11:58 AM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

A controversial bill aimed at speeding up infrastructure projects on public lands passed the U.S. Senate Thursday night and now heads to the House.

The Senate declined to vote on a flurry of last-minute amendments to the nearly 500-page text of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act — including one that would have banned data centers on public land, before voting for the third time late Thursday night. Support in the Senate eroded over the series of votes, from 73-25 on the first vote Nov. 9 to a final vote of 62-33. A bill requires a simple majority of 51 votes in the Senate to pass.

Related: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

BAAJA is co-sponsored by Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico often considered a conservation champion, and Sen. Mike Lee, the Utah Republican and architect of recent attempts to sell public land. Heinrich says BAAJA cuts red tape and will speed up renewable energy projects to help fight climate change, increase jobs, and bring down energy costs for average Americans.

Conservation advocates, however, fear it will also lock in projects many sportsmen and women have spent years fighting, like a copper-sulfide mine by the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or the Pebble Mine in Alaska’s Bristol Bay. It also may well open the door for massive data centers on public land, something most of the conservation and sporting community resoundingly oppose.

“I understand this is a big, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life earlier this week.

BAAJA proponents say it increases project certainty. Right now, one administration can reverse or cancel permits approved by a prior administration. But by limiting the back and forth between administrations the bill also drastically changes how much oversight a project can receive, even under foundational laws like the Endangered Species Act, Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act. The bill will also limit public input into projects and judicial overview.

Many of the nation’s tribes have forcefully spoken out against the bill saying it severely curtails tribal input.

“Overall, the bill, by weakening these bedrock laws, would make it far easier to fast-track AI data centers as well as fossil fuel, mining, and other extractive infrastructure. Once these projects are approved, they would be difficult to unwind,” according to the Western Environmental Law Center. “BAAJA would cause grave, generational harm to the West’s public lands, waters and wildlife, and communities.”

Heinrich has said he opposes data centers on public land.

“To be clear, BAAJA is federal legislation focused on energy infrastructure and grid connectivity,” a spokesperson told OL in an emailed satement. “It does not ‘permit’ data centers on public lands. State and local government approval is still required. The Senator’s legislation addresses the federal energy infrastructure challenges associated with a grid that cannot keep up with demand; it does not circumvent the state and local processes that determine whether specific projects move forward.”

Even conservation groups who support portions of the bill question how fast such a massive piece of legislation is moving through Congress. This is the first major permitting reform bill in decades and was introduced Sept. 30.

Read Next: Public-Land Sales, Energy Dominance, and Data Centers: What Interior’s Master Plan Really Means for Outdoorsmen

The bill now heads to the House. If representatives make any changes to the Senate version, the Senate must vote again on the bill before it heads to President Trump’s desk for his signature. The president has said he supports the bill.

This story was updated on Nov. 20 at 2:30 p.m. CST to include comment from Sen. Heinrich’s office.

Christine Peterson is a freelance writer based in southeast Wyoming covering hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation, wildlife and the environment for Outdoor Life, High Country News, National Geographic and others.

#8319. School Teacher’s First Deer with a Bow Is This 226-Inch Illinois Giant

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 1:00 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Southern Illinois school teacher Darin Hicks grew up in a hunting family, but he didn’t start hunting deer himself until just a few years ago. As his interest in deer hunting grew, he took special notice of any big bucks he spotted during his daily drives to and from school as a science teacher.

“I started seeing a large buck, but never in the day [at first],” the 40-year-old Illinois native tells Outdoor Life. “We don’t use trail cameras. But I got plenty of [phone] photos the last couple years of a really good buck — but only a few photos during the day.”

Hicks was mentoring his 9-year-old daughter, Josie, who wanted her first deer to be a buck.

“I had her out in youth season, and she could have taken a lot of does but wanted a buck. One evening we saw a buck, but it was too dark [even though it was still legal light] and Josie didn’t want to shoot in that poor light.”

Hicks thinks the buck that he and his daughter spotted that evening during the youth season may have been the giant buck he arrowed weeks later.

On Nov. 14 he hung a ladder stand near a wooded thicket full of rubs, scrapes, and plenty of trails. He set the stand for his dad, 77, to hunt during the upcoming Illinois gun opener on Nov. 20.

But that Saturday night Hicks’ wife, Katie, asked her husband if he wanted to bowhunt the stand the next day, before his father got in it the following week.

Hicks said there wasn’t much time that next morning on Sunday before they left for church. Katie said he had a good two hours to hunt from dawn until leaving for church with his family.

She had a good point, Hicks decided, and climbed into the stand the following morning of Nov. 15.

He sat for about an hour and spotted a doe with twin fawns at 150 yards. Suddenly the doe with young spooked and out stepped the giant buck Hicks had seen from afar for the last two years.

“I was shaking, found my grunt call and blew it once,” he says. “He turned and started walking toward me and my heart was pounding overtime.”

The buck came steadily closer while Hicks readied for a shot — the first time he would ever draw his bow on a whitetail.

“He walked toward me, stopped, and looked up at me at 15 yards, then he turned to head away,” Hicks says. “He started through some brush quartering away at 35 yards and I drew, released, and I heard a loud smack.”

The buck collapsed in his tracks. Hicks’ arrow had hit a bit high, but his 2-blade mechanical struck the spine and the buck didn’t get up.

Hicks managed to wrestle the nontypical out of the woods and, field-dressed, it weighed 187 pounds. His taxidermist aged the buck at 5 1/2 years, with a gross green score of 226 1/8 inches.

Read Next: Complete Shock.’ Long-Haul Trucker Hunter Tags 227-Inch Nontypical During State Park Hunt

“We all still made it to church that morning,” Hicks says. “And I even got to teach Sunday School.”

#8317. Forest Troop

Lessons in primate behavior on my first women’s surf trip.

Baboons are assholes. After leaving his birth troop at around age seven, a male will find a new one and spend his prime years trying to fang his way up the hierarchy. Once he’s gained a modicum of status, he devotes his days to terrorizing lower-ranking males and females, who only grow to half his size. Gashes, puncture wounds, and missing ears are not uncommon among baboons.

#8316. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8314. Video: Bird Dog Falls 60 Feet into Basalt Chasm, Prompting Special Rescue Mission

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 3:00 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Two unbelievable sights in one spot: a dog trapped in a deep fissure in the ground, and a crew lowering a man into that fissure to save her.

This scene unfolded in southern Idaho on Nov. 8. After a traveling bird hunter’s pointer fell some 60-feet into a basalt crack while hunting wild birds, he had to call in a professional rescue team for help.

“1,200 miles from home hunting a new bird,” wrote Kyle Stokke in an Instagram post on Nov. 12. “[I] was naively unaware of the unique dangers in these new environments.”

A post shared by Kyle Stokke (@kyle.stokke)

Stokke posted a four-minute rescue video last week. Earlier posts show him hunting upland birds with two dogs: a German shorthaired pointer and a Labrador retriever. The trio camped while traveling 1,200 miles cross-country from the Midwest to Idaho. Trouble started when the GSP, Esther, fell into a deep fissure.

“Good gracious!” an unseen rescuer says in the video. “She is down there a freaking long ways.”

Esther fell at least 60 feet. The fissure went deeper than that, but she landed on a ledge above the true bottom. In the video, you can hear her whines echo up the crack as Stokke, filming from above, reassures her.

“It’s okay Esther,” he says. “You’re a good girl.”

Magic Valley Paramedics has a dedicated unit called the Special Operations Rescue Team. SORT is a highly trained, 20-person volunteer crew specializing in low- and high-angle rope rescues.

“The biggest challenge was finding exactly where she was,” Chad Smith, SORT team leader, tells Outdoor Life. “Sound travels differently in the canyon. You could hear her so she seemed close, but she wasn’t. How sound travels in there is really deceiving. It threw us off a little bit.”

SORT averages 20 rescues a year in Twin Falls and Jerome counties. In Smith’s 15 years with SORT, the team has rescued four dogs from fissures, including another bird dog stuck in a similar crack during a previous hunting season. Esther’s rescue happened to fall on the first day of SORT’s semiannual, three-day training exercises.

“The rescue truck is pulled out and everyone is practicing anchors when the supervisor asks if we want to rescue a dog,” reads a post by the organization. “Who can say no to a dog? Training shifts gears real quick.”

The video shows the team straddling a 2-foot-wide black void hidden in flat sagebrush country.

“Wow! I can see her,” says someone offscreen as one rescuer, Trevor Churchman, is slowly lowered into the tight divide on a harness, ropes, and straps rigged to a large tripod set over the opening.

“Tell Kyle she’s doing good,” says Churchman. “She’s walking around and she’s wagging her tail.”

A few minutes later, both man and dog are hoisted out of the crack, and Esther, apparently unharmed, is handed to Stokke. He’s visibly shaking in the video and sounds emotional, but manages a “thank you” for the crew and a “whoa” to keep Esther steady, since everyone is standing near the edge.

“Okay guys, remember there’s an edge there,” a rescuer says. “We don’t have a lot of you guys on ropes.”

The two-hour rescue took place in terrain shaped by prehistoric volcanic activity. Tunnels, lava tubes, cliffs, caves, and crevices run through much of the area’s undeveloped public land. (If that’s hard to picture, think of the better-known volcanic landscape at Craters of the Moon National Monument and Preserve, 90 miles north of Twin Falls.)

Water filters through the porous basalt rock formations, creating seeps, springs, and waterfalls that feed the Snake River, which has carved a deep canyon that’s home to the dramatic spray of Shoshone Falls.

“When hiking around the canyon, cracks in the rock can be quite deep,” the rescue team warns. “This one was deeper than 45 feet. We could not see the bottom, and they can fill with tumbleweeds making them look like level ground. So watch your step.”

Read Next: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Finally Resigns as Plea Deal in Elk Poaching Scandal Draws Hunter Outrage

It’s rough, remote country that attracts extreme adventurers like BASE jumpers. And it can surprise even experienced bird hunters, such as Stokke, who assume they’re hunting in relatively flat country.

Kris Millgate is a multimedia journalist based in eastern Idaho. She’s a fly fisher, a bird hunter and an avid seeker of awkward moments. Read and watch more of her work at tightlinemedia.com

#8312. Simms Rip Line PRO Review: We Tested This Heavy-Duty Fishing Rain Gear in Downpours and High Winds

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 3:54 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Simms has long been an industry staple for fishing apparel, most notably waders and outerwear. I’ve tested and reviewed many Simms products, including its Challenger lineup of rain gear. While that gear has always performed well, its target market is clear: dedicated recreational anglers. I’ve never bothered to test how Simms outerwear handles the trials and tribulations of everyday use by commercial deckhands or saltwater captains because, frankly, why would I? That’s not the audience it’s intended for, and I wouldn’t expect rain gear designed for landlocked fly anglers to hold up for someone used to hauling crab traps in salt spray and freezing rain all day.

Enter Simms’ new Rip Line Pro series of rain gear, the company’s first attempt at a truly hardcore jacket and bibs designed specifically for watermen. The Rip Line Pro series forgoes much of the aesthetic and, shall we say, fanciness of Simms’ standard recreation-oriented rain gear in favor of pure, rugged functionality. From the moment you see the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs, it’s clear they aren’t meant for a hike down to your favorite blue-ribbon trout stream. Pick them up and feel them in hand, and that point is driven home. This is not casual rain gear, and it doesn’t sacrifice performance for looks. It’s designed for abuse of the highest order, the kind dished out by Mother Nature on the open sea.

So, how does it handle that? The look and feel right out of the box make a promise, but does the Rip Line Pro series deliver? To find out, I spent a few weeks putting this gear through the wringer in one of the best testing grounds I could think of: the Chesapeake Bay in late fall and early winter. Read on to see how the Rip Line Pro performed.

When it comes to testing gear, sometimes the timing doesn’t line up. Given the monthslong drought in the Mid-Atlantic leading up to my test, I was worried that might be the case here. As it turned out, that worry was misplaced. Exactly one day after the Rip Line Pro gear arrived, the forecast called for an epic deluge paired with extreme wind and storms. It was the perfect blend of miserable fishing conditions for testing rain gear. Lucky me.

The forecast proved accurate, and the weather was extreme, almost to a fault. I spent the first few hours of the morning sheltering from lightning under a dockhouse on the water. The Rip Line Pro gear will protect you from a lot, but I don’t think “lightning strike” is on the list. Thankfully, the electrical portion of the storm passed, and I had the rest of the day to fish in a constant downpour and gusting wind.

After a few hours of fishing from a kayak in the rain and getting sprayed with salt water, the first thing I checked was the areas where most rain gear performs worst: the wrists, neck, and ankles. These are typically the hardest spots to protect because they offer a direct path for water to get beneath the rain gear, and they still need to allow some comfort and range of motion. The Rip Line Pro did an outstanding job of keeping moisture out of all three. The wrists and forearms were the most impressive. They feature an extended 1-millimeter neoprene cuff beneath the outer layer that lets this jacket perform almost like a full dry top. Not only does it keep rain out, but the neoprene cuff creates a seal that kept water from flowing down the sleeve even when my arm was fully submerged. I was equally impressed by the neck. While it doesn’t have the full neoprene seal of the sleeves, the hood design and zipper-and-Velcro combination created an impressively form-fitting seal that kept water from dripping down my back or chest. Finally, the ankle cuffs on the bibs did an excellent job of keeping spray and rainwater away from my feet. I was wearing ankle-height deck boots, and the leg cuffs paired perfectly with them to create an angled seal where no water could enter.

Next, I inspected the storage, namely the various dry pockets on both the jacket and bibs. Each has a well-designed, easily accessible exterior pocket sealed by a watertight zipper and tucked beneath a Velcro storm flap for extra protection. Exterior pockets on rain gear are always a gamble, but accessible waterproof storage is important. The pockets on the Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs performed exceptionally well, even after I opened and closed them many times throughout the day to reach various items. Nothing seeped through the pockets to the interior of the suit, and the pockets kept everything inside them dry and functional.

Dry storage and adjustable cuffs matter, but ultimately the most important job of rain gear is keeping you dry all day long. While I was impressed with how well the Rip Line Pro kept water out of various areas throughout the day, the real test would be how wet and cold I got after fishing in rain and wind for upward of 12 hours.

The answer? Not very. For me, the most impressive part of this gear is the overall protection it offered from the elements. After we returned to the boat ramp and loaded our gear, it was time to strip off the rain suit and inspect the damage. No matter how dry you think you are, a bit of unforeseen moisture usually gets through any rain gear after a long day. Apart from a few wet spots where my shirt had been exposed during the day, I was basically bone-dry. The jacket and bibs also did a great job of blocking wind chill. I had underestimated how well that was working during the day, but looking back, I realized how much the gear kept the wind from affecting my comfort. Not that I needed confirmation, but watching my fishing partners shiver miserably and wring out sopping undershirts provided a sense of warm relief, both physically and emotionally.

Protection from the elements, plain and simple. I’ve worn many bibs and rain jackets over the years, some designed for comfort and others for function. The Rip Line Pro does the best job I’ve found of marrying the two, though function is still clearly the priority.

Once you’re fully suited up, this rain gear makes you feel practically invincible, protected by an impenetrable shell of armor. I’m not saying it’s bulletproof, but I could feel an unrealistic sense of confidence building while I wore it. The materials not only kept me bone-dry through a full day of torrential rain but also provided exceptional wind protection during gusts upward of 30 knots. When it comes to protection from extreme water and wind, the Rip Line Pro series is as good as it gets.

With extreme weather protection as the focus, it’s easy to understand why some other features take a back seat. That said, there are still a few areas I’d like to see Simms improve.

The most noticeable is the lack of mobility. The four-layer construction and fully waterproof material make this gear weatherproof, but they also make it rather cumbersome. Simms added articulation points and adjustable areas where possible, but there’s still room for improvement. At times, I felt a bit like a piece of vacuum-sealed meat, or a video game character bolted into a mech suit. Yes, I felt invincible, but I also had a harder time than I care to admit squatting to grab a sandwich from the cooler.

Insulation is another area that could be better. The Rip Line Pro gear does an incredible job of protecting you from water and wind, but it doesn’t have much interior insulation for true winter use. That’s easy to offset by layering proper cold-weather clothing underneath, but I could see a built-in cold-weather liner helping. Perhaps Simms will release a “winter” edition of the Rip Line Pro in the future with a wool liner or something similar.

The Rip Line Pro series of rain gear is not for everyone. In fact, I would say the target market for this gear is fairly narrow. Most casual anglers and outdoor enthusiasts can get by with less extreme, less expensive rain gear and never have an issue. While this gear is fantastic at keeping you dry, I could see it being overkill for an after-work outing during a light summer shower.

However, what the Rip Line Pro series is designed to do, it does extremely well, and the people who need this type of gear will appreciate it. The Rip Line Pro series is built for serious anglers and people who spend as much time on the water as on dry land. As with any gear in the fishing space, the more purpose-built something becomes, the less universal appeal it tends to have. That said, if you fish as much as I do, serious rain gear becomes less a matter of convenience and more a matter of necessity. The Rip Line Pro jacket and bibs offer the type of performance and functionality I value, and I’m sure many other anglers, deckhands, and charter captains who try them will agree.

#8309. Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 4:45 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

If you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list. Its classic flooded hardwoods and bayous along with the state’s rich rice and grain fields, lure massive flights of puddle ducks and geese to its hallowed waters every year. This has made Arkansas stand out above other southern states as the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway.

Yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak. A historic drought has many duck hunters worried ahead of the Nov. 21 opener, as the serious lack of water could bring duck hunting to a standstill. Duck hunters on both public and private land may have some serious decisions to make to safeguard ducks and future duck seasons.

For 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades. Every corner of the state is under a severe drought status, with some areas being more than 20 inches behind in cumulative rainfall totals.

To put the drought in perspective, this is slated to be the state’s third-driest October through January since record keeping began in 1895.

This leaves the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission with very little water to spare, to the point where the agency expects it will only be able to flood around 40 of its more than 70 moist-soil public-land hunting units.

“In my 50 years of duck hunting in Arkansas, I don’t remember it ever being as dry as this,” says Brent Birch, founder of Arkansas’ Greenhead magazine. “It’s been this way all summer and well into the fall. And even with the prospects of a Super El Niño, we have nothing the forecast that says it’s going to resolve anytime soon.”

Without an incredible amount of rainfall in a short amount of time, Birch and other waterfowlers around the state are worried not only about not having places to hunt, but that the ducks may not even show up.

“So far, we are seeing a few groups of gadwalls, pintails, and other early migrating ducks but not in anything close to their usual numbers,” Birch says. “And when it comes to incoming mallards, you can pretty much forget it. It’s just too dry for them. The fact is the closer it gets to 2027 under these conditions, the worse the entire duck season is going to be. And if we don’t start getting some wet weather soon to push ducks down here, we’re looking at a poor outlook for the entire season.”

The reason that Arkansas waterfowl hunting is so good is that it lies at the north end of the historic feeding grounds for ducks and geese in the Mississippi Flyway. Once the cold sets in around their spring and summer breeding grounds in Canada, the birds come south to binge on Arkansas’ rich wetlands throughout the winter. However, with the current drought, the fear is that the incoming ducks will be forced to fly elsewhere.

“Ducks coming south to Arkansas aren’t like ducks in northern states,” says Ducks Unlimited Arkansas regional biologist Jake Spears, who lives in Jonesboro. “Northern birds are more apt to feed in dry fields so long as they have a body of water to roost on nearby. However, in the Southern U.S., they stop feeding in fields and primarily feed in water. They look for things like water plants and waste grains in flooded fields, which Arkansas currently just doesn’t have.”

Spears worries that many ducks are going to fly to Arkansas and then be forced to turn northward again or keep driving south.

“The ducks need food so they may go to Louisiana, or Kansas, or Missouri — wherever they can find that food source,” says Spears. “Which is going to leave both public-land duck hunters and even most hunting clubs just completely out of luck.”

Private-land duck-hunting clubs are a popular option for many Arkansas hunters and visiting nonresidents, as even during droughts, most clubs can pump water to create duck habitat and attract birds. The 2026 drought has been so bad, however, that many clubs won’t even have the water to pump.

This is especially troubling to some public-land waterfowl hunters, who worry that the private hunting clubs that can still pump water may end up attracting what few ducks do make it to Arkansas. This could result in a season that benefits the haves over the have-nots.

“I think hunting clubs are the only thing that’s going to make Arkansas appealing for ducks right now,” Spears says. “Most of the smaller rivers, sloughs, and backwaters we have on public land can be walked across in flip-flops right now. So the clubs that have the option to flood fields and create habitat are where the birds are going to be. But with the water table so low, clubs with the ability to pump will be few and far between, so any ducks that do show up during the season are going to have to be babied quite a bit.”

The fact is that if the drought continues in Arkansas, duck hunters on both public and private land alike are going to have to weigh their priorities. Drought conditions are going to be tough on ducks that migrate through Arkansas, and hunting pressure will make surviving the migration harder even for birds that aren’t killed.

This leaves duck hunters with a choice to make.

“It’s going to come down to responsible management on all sides because if we want to maintain the ducks we have, we have to be careful with them,” Birch says. “There are several components to management. It’s not just hunting and the noise of guns, we must be careful disturbing the ducks in any capacity. Your vehicle is an issue because you’re going to bump ducks going in and out of your hunting area, and you’re going to have to be real careful with how many days you hunt and how many hours you hunt in a day, because you’re going to have to let the birds rest.”

With Arkansas’ duck season lasting a total of 51 days with two relatively short splits, hunters looking to limit out consistently are going to be putting serious pressure on what will already be a limited resource.

So instead of hunting hard, both Birch and Spears recommend self-imposed bag limits and time on the water so that the resource can continue to both be conserved and shared.

“My suggestion to any duck hunter in Arkansas is that if you have ducks on your property, take care of them,” says Spears. “With the limited resources, they aren’t going to be able to handle a lot of pressure. You’re going to have to limit how much you hunt and how many birds you shoot, and not be afraid to cut your hunt short. Get a few birds and then leave so the ducks can get back to the water to feed.”

Read Next: Has Hot Cropping Ruined Duck Hunting? Here’s What the Data and Biologists Say About How Flooded Corn Affects Waterfowl Migration

While there is hope that conditions will change, the fact is that the whole of Arkansas’ 2026 duck season may be a nonstarter for many hunters. That short-term pain, however, could help future duck seasons look a little brighter. Spears and Birch are hopeful for a future where water and the waterfowl will eventually return, filling the skies and waterways like flowing veins and once again making Arkansas the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway itself.

“We need to be good stewards of the resource,” urges Spears. “Hunters should do everything they can to keep [ducks] around and not shoot them off what water we do have.”

#8308. The World’s Most Cinematic Trail Running Is Hidden Above the Arctic Circle

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

On my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

The Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!)

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

The vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

Lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

It’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

#8305. Budget Ski Gear Is Hiding at Costco, and Some of It Is From Brands We Trust

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

You don’t need to pay premium prices to build a ski-day layering system. (Photo: Re Wikstrom)

Overview: These editor-approved Costco ski gear picks come from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Head, and Dakine. We flag what you give up at each price, so beginners and casual skiers can shop smart. Skiers facing harsh weather may still want premium shells and insulation. Costco’s stock changes fast, so grab what you want early.

With groceries and gas so pricey, it’s no wonder so many of us are turning to Costco. Everyone knows the warehouse is a deal machine for electronics, home goods, and tires, but this time of year, the aisles are also stocked with a surprising array of ski gear at steep discounts.

Plenty of skiers assume outdoor gear from big-box stores and other non-specialty retailers can’t be trusted. At Costco, that’s not necessarily true. The warehouse pulls in items from brands skiers know, like Smith, Spyder, Dakine, Eddie Bauer, and Head, and its seasoned members know a steal when they see one. A Spyder full-zip sweater jacket for $30 or less? That goes straight in the cart. Buy now, try on at home: Costco’s “satisfaction guaranteed” return policy means you can easily take back whatever doesn’t work out.

The catch: buying ski gear from a warehouse means making compromises. A specialty ski shop has gear with premium features like name-brand insulation and weatherproof materials (and premium prices to match). If you’re outside for hours in gnarly weather, you may need those technical features to stay warm and dry. But casual skiers, beginners, and kids will find plenty of choices at Costco, and experts can find some gems, too. It’s the perfect place for a comfy fleece, a reasonably priced heated vest, a MIPS helmet, affordable gloves and goggles, and après-ski accessories. SKI recommends the following items, but act fast because, like a powder day, the goods won’t last.

Fine print: you’ll need a Costco membership to snag any of these, so factor the annual fee into your budget.

Smith is a specialty-shop staple, so finding the Survey on the Costco website is a legit surprise. This all-mountain lid pairs MIPS with Koroyd zones that keep the weight down. An integrated ChromaPop visor stands in for goggles and works with glasses, and a dial fine-tunes the fit.

Compromise: There really isn’t one. You get a top-shelf helmet at Costco pricing (it retails for around $260 elsewhere). If you weren’t a visor-helmet person before now, maybe you just became one?

This is the budget way to get a MIPS-equipped helmet on your head, and it hits the feature checklist. Three-stage vents let you dump heat on sunny laps, the earpads come out when spring arrives, and a built-in goggle lock keeps most goggles from sliding off the back. An adjustable retention system helps dial in the fit, and it comes in four sizes, small through extra large.

Compromise: You get the safety and venting, but not the luxe features of a premium helmet, like a plush lining or a magnetic chin buckle.

Magnetic lens swap systems are usually a perk of pricier goggles, but Nordik includes one in these affordable goggles. The HOD’s magnetic system lets you pop lenses in and out in seconds, and the box includes a second, low-light lens so you’re covered when the sun disappears. The oversized spherical lens has anti-fog treatment and UV400 protection, and the roomy OTG frame fits over large glasses and runs medium to large. A carrying case is thrown in, too.

Compromise: You’re not getting top-of-the-line lenses with light-adapting tech, so you’ll swap lenses by hand when conditions change.

When it comes to ski mittens, leather is king, and getting a deerskin outer at Costco prices is a serious bargain. Deerskin naturally sheds water and wind and holds up to season after season of abuse, the kind of toughness synthetic shells struggle to match. These pair that shell with 150-gram 3M Thinsulate and a waterproof, breathable insert. The extended gauntlet cuff, with an adjustable strap and cinch cord, seals out powder.

Compromise: You’re not getting a branded waterproof membrane like Gore-Tex, so don’t count on premium storm performance.

You can outfit the entire family with Head’s ski gloves thanks to a size run ranging from XS to XL. With a combination of lightweight and breathable insulation and a waterproof/windproof insert, the gloves keep hands warm on milder ski days, with an exterior zippered pocket for handwarmers. Touchscreen technology means you can access your smartphone without removing your gloves.

Compromise: If you spend less than $25 on gloves, don’t expect them to hold up to prolonged exposure to super cold temps or wet weather. (You’d have to spend at least $100 more for that.) Durability may be a weakness too, as the soft polyester material on the palm could peel off with use.

Dakine, born in Hawaii in 1979 and now a fixture in ski and snowboard shops, is another name you won’t expect to find next to the paper towels. This insulated midweight jacket has the details kids actually use: an inner powder skirt, a storm shield inside the hood, and two zippered side pockets. The hood comes off when it’s not needed, and sizes run XS–XL for the growth spurts that make buying premium kids’ gear hurt.

Pair it with the snow pants for a budget head-to-toe outfit. The insulated pants are wind and water resistant, with snow gaiters and elastic grippers that keep boots from letting in snow, plus a Velcro-adjustable waist for the in-between sizes. Two front slant pockets, a side zip pocket and scuff guards at the hems round it out.

Compromise: With the jacket, you’re giving up the proven weather protection of a premium kids’ shell. The jacket lists no waterproof rating or sealed seams, so think dry-snow resort days, not PNW storm skiing. For the pants, water resistant isn’t waterproof, so don’t count on these for skiing and playing in wet snow.

Eddie Bauer has been making outdoor clothing and gear since 1920, when Eddie Bauer opened his Sports Shop in Seattle, close to Costco’s headquarters in Washington. The hooded full-zip fleece nods to the days when a heavyweight midlayer doubled as a jacket. Layered under a shell for ski days, or standalone, the 100 percent polyester fleece has a soft and comfy kid-friendly hand feel.

Compromise: This isn’t a lightweight performance fleece for easy layering under a ski jacket; its heavyweight fuzzy fabric makes it better suited to après play and around-town wear.

At $50, the 32 Degrees Rechargeable Heated Vest is your gateway into heated ski gear. It’s the perfect marriage of value and warmth, and fits well over base and midlayers. Fleece-lined and lightweight, the vest comes pre-wired with four heat panels, two in front and two in back. A palm-sized battery pack, rechargeable through a USB-C charging cable, powers the heat, offering a little extra warmth for chilly chairlift rides.

Compromise: If you pay under $50, don’t expect the design and functionality of a $150 vest. Expect relatively short battery life, and make sure to research how to turn it on. Plus, all your friends will know when you have your vest turned on thanks to a red “Heat” logo. But embrace this: You will be warmer than them.

32 Degrees’ mission is to provide value and comfort, which is exactly why Costco skiers should take a hard look at the 32 Degrees Women’s Fleece. The high-pile fleece is not only soft and comfy, but it traps in body heat, while the 1/4-zip offers some venting. The kangaroo pocket doubles as a handwarmer, but what women may appreciate most is that the round-bottom hem looks cool with tights or snowpants.

Compromise: The sleeves are known to run long.

Spyder, founded in 1978 in Boulder, Colorado, is one of the most recognizable ski brands around the world. The Spyder Full Zip Sweater Jacket remains the quintessential ski town staple around every ski resort. Wear it as a standalone piece, or use the durable, heavyweight jacket as a midlayer under a ski jacket. Burly zippers abound with the full front zippered closure, a chest pocket and side storage pocket.

Compromise: The heavyweight fabric on this sweater jacket makes it a bit hefty for aerobic activities. Since it leans more après than technical, don’t expect great wind protection or core warmth.

Create a cool vibe during your après-ski tailgate with the Soundcore Boom 3i Outdoor Bluetooth speaker. Even if snowflakes fall, the waterproof and dustproof speaker keeps the beat without worrying about the elements. The rechargeable battery comes with a USB-C cable and holds a charge for up to 16 hours. At the end of a great ski day, the beat-synced lightshow hypes you up for more.

Compromise: There isn’t one.  You get a tough, waterproof speaker at a reasonable price. It’s not a premium speaker for audiophiles, but it will get the job done.

One of the best feelings in life is taking off your ski boots and sliding your feet into something comfortable. Enter the Kirkland Signature Unisex Slipper. Kirkland, Costco’s signature brand, named for the Seattle suburb where Costco began, is not to be scoffed at because it often stands in for other more expensive brand-name items like Uggs. Case in point—the Shearling Slipper features genuine sheepskin shearling, an embroidered collar and a lightweight outsole grippy enough for mountain hut floors or ski area parking lots.

Compromise: You get the shearling-lined comfort of a premium slipper like an Ugg, but not the sole. Kirkland’s outsole is lightweight, so these are for hut floors and well-maintained parking lots.
